summary: This unit teaches a Level 3 welder or leading hand to help prepare and carry out a workshop's operational plan. You will write SMART objectives and KPIs, consult the team, work out the people, machines, materials and money needed, help with budgets and variances, manage risks, support staffing and training, and monitor and report progress honestly.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). Many Level 3 welders become leading hands, charge hands or supervisors. This unit teaches you to **support the operational plan** of your workshop or section: help prepare it, put it into action with your team, keep track of how it is going, and report on it.

An operational plan turns the owner's big goals into the week-by-week work of the shop: what will be made, by whom, by when, with which machines, materials and money, and how you will know it is on track. You do not usually write the whole plan alone, but you supply the facts, lead the team that carries it out, and are often the first to see when it starts to slip.

**Who it is for:** trainees on the Welding Level 3 programme at HEART/NSTA Trust and other training centres, and welders and fabricators who lead a team, a shift or a site crew. The examples come from fabrication shops, but the same methods work in any workshop.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means at work
rows: Say what an operational plan is, how it links to the business (strategic) plan, and what it contains.
Help write SMART objectives and choose key performance indicators (KPIs) with targets.
Gather facts, ideas and concerns from the team and other stakeholders, and feed them into the plan.
Work out the people, hours, skills, machines, materials and money needed; compare them with what is available; close the gaps; ask for extra resources with figures.
Help prepare a budget, compare actual spending with it, and work out variances.
Identify and rate risks, and plan controls and contingency plans.
Help recruit, induct and develop staff, and deal fairly with performance problems.
Track the KPIs, find the causes of shortfalls, agree corrective action, and report honestly and on time.
Keep plans, decisions and staff information accurate, current and secure.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on plans, objectives and KPIs, consultation, resources, budgets, risk, staffing, monitoring, reporting, records and the law.

A **written paper** with short answers (terms and simple sums) and essays, for example explaining an operational plan, consulting the team, choosing KPIs, finding resources, monitoring, managing risk, staffing, budgets, improvement and the monthly report.

**Two group practicals**: drafting a month's operational plan for the workshop and presenting it; and comparing a month's results with the plan, writing a variance report and presenting it in a role-played meeting with management.

blocks.note: Practise the sums: percentage of target, utilisation, variance in J$ and as a percentage, hours needed against hours available, and quarterly budgets. Write each step down and check it a second way.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Operational plans and where they fit

head: Plan
Time span
What it covers
Example
rows: The whole business: its direction, markets, growth and big investments. Set by the owners or directors
Grow gate and grille sales by 25% in three years, and win school and church roofing work
A month, a quarter or a year
One section or team: what it will do, who does it, when, and with which resources. Prepared by managers with supervisors and the team
Workshop plan for January–March: deliver 36 roof trusses and 40 grilles, 95% on time, rework below 4%
Who does which job today and this week. Set by the supervisor
The job board on the workshop wall

blocks.p: Each level puts the one above it into action. The strategic plan says **where** the business wants to go; the operational plan says **how** your section will do its share of that, day to day. If the business plan aims to win roofing work, the workshop's operational plan sets the trusses to be made, the people and machines needed, the budget and the quality checks.

head: Part
What it says
rows: What the team must achieve, written as SMART objectives, with the measures and targets that show progress
Every task, each with one named person responsible
When each task starts and finishes, often shown as a bar (Gantt) chart, with deadlines and milestones
People and hours, skills, machines, materials and consumables, and money
The expected costs by heading and by month
What could go wrong, how likely and how serious it is, how to prevent it, and what to do if it happens
Inspection points built into the schedule; the safety controls the work needs
What is measured, how often, by whom, and who reports to whom
When the plan will be looked at again, and changed if needed

blocks.h: Your role as supervisor or leading hand

ul: Supply facts and ideas when the plan is being prepared: real job times, machine condition, stock, skills, problems.
Consult your team, and make sure their knowledge reaches the plan.
Explain the plan to the team, so everyone knows their part and why it matters.
Organise the daily work to the plan.
Monitor progress against the KPIs and the budget, and act when results fall short.
Report accurately and on time, and suggest changes when things change.
Keep the records the plan needs.

blocks.h: Working within the law and policies

blocks.p: An operational plan must follow the law and the workplace's own policies, so that the work is safe, fair and legal. That includes **health and safety law** (a safe workplace, safe machines, PPE and training), **employment law** (hours, overtime pay, holidays with pay, fair treatment and no discrimination), **environmental rules** (waste, noise, fumes), the **data protection law** (personal information about staff and customers), the **contracts** with clients and suppliers, and workplace policies such as purchasing approval limits, overtime approval and quality procedures.

blocks.note: A target that can only be met by breaking a safety rule, the law or a policy is a bad target. Re-plan the work or report the problem: never drop the rule.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Letter
Stands for
The question to ask
rows: Is it clear exactly what is to be achieved, and by whom?
Is there a number, so we will know whether it has been met?
Can it be done with the people, time and money we have, and has the team agreed to it?
Does it help the business plan?

head: Weak objective
SMART objective
rows: "Cut the average fit-up time for a gate frame from 50 to 40 minutes by 30 June."
"No lost-time injuries this quarter, and every near miss reported within 24 hours."
"Deliver 95% of jobs on or before the agreed date each month from April."
"Keep spending on discs and wire within J$45,000 a month for the next three months."

blocks.p: A **key performance indicator (KPI)** is a measure of progress towards an objective. Choose a few (often four to six), each with a clear formula, a source of data, a target, how often it is measured, and who is responsible for it. KPIs turn goals into numbers, so everyone can see progress and problems are spotted early.

head: KPI
How it is worked out
Data from
Example target
rows: Jobs delivered by the agreed date ÷ jobs delivered × 100
Items passing inspection with no rework ÷ items inspected × 100
Hours spent on rework in the month
Units made per week, or per labour hour

blocks.p: Some KPIs warn you early (jobs behind schedule this week), others report after the event (last month's on-time delivery). Use both: the early ones give you time to act.

head: Question
Working
Answer
rows: The target was 60 grilles; 52 were made. What percentage of the target was reached?
168 brackets were made in 48 labour hours. What is the output per hour?
Rework fell from 25 hours to 18 hours a month. What is the percentage fall?
4 items of 125 inspected needed rework. What is the first-time pass rate?

blocks.p: A **stakeholder** is any person or group with an interest in the plan, or affected by it. The people who do the work know how long tasks really take and what gets in the way, so consulting them makes the plan realistic.

head: Stakeholder
What they know or need
How to consult them
rows: Real job times, problems, the skills they have, ideas
Team meeting, one-to-one talks, a simple suggestion sheet
Stock levels, supplier lead times, prices
Machine condition and the service schedule
Meetings; a draft plan for comment

flow: Explain what the business wants to achieve and the draft targets
Ask specific questions: how long does this take, what gets in the way, what do you need?
Listen, and write the answers down
Check the facts, and use the good ideas in the plan
Tell people what was used, and why some ideas were not
Share the final plan and confirm everyone knows their part

blocks.p: Consultation matters because it gives **realistic targets**, builds **commitment** (people support a plan they helped to make), finds **risks early**, and brings out **better ideas**. It also shows respect for the team's experience.

blocks.note: Not everyone speaks up in a meeting, and some people find forms hard to fill in. Talk to the quieter members one to one, and accept ideas by word of mouth as well as on paper.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Resources: people, machines, materials and money

blocks.p: An operational plan usually covers four types of resource: **people**, **equipment**, **materials** and **money**. Start from the plan's targets, work out what they need, compare that with what you have, and close the gap.

flow: Hours needed: units to make × hours per unit, plus the other work that must go on
Hours available: people × hours each, less leave, training and other duties
The gap: hours needed − hours available
Skills: compare the skills the work needs with the skills each person has
Choose how to close any gap

head: Step
Worked example
rows: 45 balcony rails at 4 welding hours each = 180 hours, over 2 weeks = 90 hours a week
130 ÷ 40 = 3.25: round **up** to 4 welders, or cover the extra 10 hours another way

head: Option
Points to think about
rows: Re-schedule or change the order of work
Costs nothing; check other due dates
Move people from less urgent work
That work slips; agree it with the manager
Costs more (overtime rates); fatigue; employment law on hours; must be approved
Check their qualifications; give them an induction
For example cutting or galvanising; check quality and lead time
Agree a new date with the client
Only with the manager's agreement, and early
The long-term answer to a gap that will not go away

blocks.p: **Utilisation = hours used ÷ hours available × 100.** A bandsaw available 40 hours a week and used for 22 hours is 55% utilised. If a new job adds 14 hours, it rises to 36 ÷ 40 = 90%. A machine running near 90–100% is a **bottleneck**: one breakdown stops the work behind it, so plan maintenance carefully, keep spares, and know your back-up.
The plan sets **minimum stock levels** for consumables such as wire, electrodes, discs and gas, so the shop does not run out and stop work. A simple **reorder level** is:

**Reorder level = usage per week × supplier lead time in weeks + safety stock.** Example: cutting discs are used at 25 a week, the supplier takes 2 weeks, and the shop keeps 20 as safety stock: 25 × 2 + 20 = **70 discs**. When stock falls to 70, order more.

blocks.note: Most steel is imported, so lead times can stretch when ships are delayed, before Christmas, and in the hurricane season. Agree lead times with suppliers in writing, order early for big jobs, and keep a little more safety stock in those periods.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Managers say yes to clear figures, not to complaints. A short written request (a business case) sets out:

head: Part
Example: a second MIG set
rows: A second MIG set for bay 3
The one MIG set is used 38 of 40 hours a week; welders wait for it about 12 hours a week
Overtime on the existing set; MMAW instead (slower on thin sheet); hiring a set
Two quotes; the best is J$420,000
12 hours a week saved × J$1,500 an hour = J$18,000 a week, so it pays for itself in about 23 weeks
Before the grille contract starts on 1 March

blocks.p: Send it through the business's approval process, and follow the purchasing rules.

A **budget** is the plan in money: the expected spending (and sometimes income) for a period, by cost heading and by month. The supervisor helps prepare it from the workload, past records and current prices, and then helps keep spending within it.

flow: Start from the plan's workload for the period
Look at past spending records for similar work
Get current prices and quotes, and check them with purchasing
Set the figures out by cost heading and by month
Add a small contingency for the unexpected
Agree it with your manager and get it approved

blocks.p: A **variance** is the difference between the budgeted figure and the actual figure. **Variance = actual − budget.** As a percentage: **variance ÷ budget × 100.** For costs, spending over budget is an **adverse** (unfavourable) variance and spending under budget is **favourable**. For income, more than budget is favourable.
Always work out **why** a variance happened before deciding what to do:

ul: **Price**: the supplier charged more per unit.
**Usage**: more was used than planned, through waste, rework or poor settings.
**Volume**: more (or less) work was done than planned, so spending should change too.
**Timing**: a bill was paid earlier or later than planned.
**Mistakes**: an invoice was put under the wrong heading.

blocks.note: Under budget is not always good news. Check that maintenance was not skipped, PPE not left unbought, stock not run down, and invoices not simply still to come.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Then act: reduce waste, re-plan the work, renegotiate prices, or report early to your manager with the reasons and a suggestion. Follow the approval rules for spending, and never hide an overspend by moving it to another heading.

**Cash flow** is the timing of money coming into and going out of the business. A job can make a profit and still leave the business short of cash if steel and wages must be paid long before the client pays.

head: Month
Without a deposit
With a 40% deposit (J$600,000)
rows: Pay steel J$600,000 and wages J$300,000
Same costs; deposit of J$600,000 comes in
Pay wages J$300,000: the business is now J$1,200,000 out of pocket
Pay wages J$300,000: J$600,000 out of pocket
Client pays the balance of J$900,000

blocks.p: The business protects its cash with deposits, stage payments, careful timing of purchases, supplier credit, and an overdraft arranged before it is needed. Your part as supervisor: warn the manager early about big purchases, do not order more stock than the plan needs, and get finished work signed off quickly so the invoice can go out.

sections.title: Putting the plan into action: scheduling, monitoring and reporting

blocks.p: Explain the plan at a team meeting, not just by pinning it on the wall. Go through the objectives, the targets, each person's tasks and the dates, and **why** they matter. Answer questions, and put a one-page summary or poster where everyone can see it.

A **bar chart** (Gantt chart) lists the tasks down the side and the weeks across the top, with a bar for each task's start and finish. It shows who does what each week, which tasks depend on others (you cannot weld before cutting), the milestones, and the inspection points built into the schedule.

ul: Collect the figures regularly from job cards, time sheets, inspection records, stock records, invoices and the incident log.
Plot each KPI on a progress chart with its target line, so anyone can see at a glance whether work is on track.
Walk the workshop: see for yourself what is happening and talk to the team.
Hold a short daily or weekly review, and share the results with the team.
Review the plan regularly (for example monthly), and also whenever something important changes.

flow: Spot it: a KPI below target, or a task behind schedule
Get the facts from the records and the people involved
Find the cause, for example by asking "why?" until you reach it
Agree a corrective action with the team, with an owner and a date
Act within your authority; report what is beyond it, with the facts and a suggestion
Check that the action worked
Record it and update the plan

head: Why?
Answer
rows: Why was output 15% below target in week 3?
MIG bay 2 was stopped for two days.
Why did that stop the bay for two days?
There was no spare, and it had to be ordered.
Planned maintenance and spares were not in the plan.
Add monthly MIG servicing to the plan and keep a spare drive unit; owner: leading hand; by the end of the month.

blocks.p: The plan is not fixed for ever. When someone suggests a better way, try it on a small scale, measure the result, and if it works, add it to the plan and the procedures (the Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle). The unit on supporting continuous improvement covers this in depth.

head: A monthly report includes
Example
rows: "On track for output; behind on delivery; over budget on overtime."
A chart of weekly output with the target line
Each heading, with variances in J$ and %
Causes of shortfalls, with the action, owner and date
Risks growing, extra resources needed, training given
Ideas that worked, and who deserves credit

ul: Use plain words, short headings, tables and simple charts; keep it to one or two pages.
Make the figures accurate, and send it on time, so problems are fixed before they grow.
Date it, and keep a copy on file.

blocks.note: Report the true figures, even when they are bad. Changing figures to make a KPI look met is dishonest, may be fraud, and leaves managers deciding on false information. If someone asks you to do it, refuse and report the true figures.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A **risk** is something that might happen and would affect the plan. Managing risk means finding the risks early, deciding which matter most, making them less likely or less serious, and knowing what you will do if they happen.

flow: Identify the risks with the team, using past records and experience
Rate each one: likelihood × consequence
Plan **controls** that make the risk less likely or less serious
Write a **contingency plan**: what to do if it happens anyway
Record it all in a risk register, with an owner for each risk
Review the register regularly, and when things change

blocks.p: In a simple **risk matrix**, likelihood and consequence are each scored from 1 (rare, or minor) to 5 (almost certain, or severe). The risk level is **likelihood × consequence**. For example, scores of 1–4 may be treated as low, 5–9 as medium and 10–25 as high. Deal with the high risks first.

A **control** acts **before** the event, to make it less likely or less serious: servicing a machine, ordering steel early, training a second person. A **contingency plan** says what you will do **if** the risk happens: move the work to another machine, use the generator, call in a temporary welder.

head: Risk
Controls (before)
Contingency plan (if it happens)
rows: Hurricane or tropical storm (season 1 June to 30 November)
Check the roof, gutters and drains before the season; stock up early; back up records; insurance
Storm plan: secure the shop, switch off power and gas, raise stock off the floor, re-plan deliveries and tell clients
Surge protection; plan heavy welding around announced outages
Engine-driven welder or generator; re-order the work
Order early; minimum stock; more than one supplier
Use approved alternative sizes (with written approval); re-order the jobs
Move the work to another machine; hire one
Train a second person in each key skill
Steel price or exchange rate rises
Short validity on quotes; buy steel when the job is confirmed
Talk to the client about the contract terms; revise later quotes
Safe systems of work, PPE, training, supervision
First aid, emergency plan, report and investigate
Spare sets; report to police and insurer

blocks.p: A **risk register** lists each risk with its owner, its score, its controls, its contingency plan, its review date and its current status.

blocks.note: Before each hurricane season, run through the storm plan with the team: who secures what, where stock and machines go, how to contact each other, and how work restarts. Check the plan again when a storm is forecast.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: People: staffing, induction, development and records

flow: From the plan, work out the hours and skills needed, and compare them with the team
Help write the job description (the duties) and the person specification (skills, qualifications such as NCTVET Level 2 or 3 welding, pipe or aluminium experience)
Help shortlist and interview, following the business's fair recruitment policy
Ask every candidate the same job-related questions, and use a practical welding test where it fits
Keep notes, and never let race, religion, sex, age, disability or other personal matters decide
The authorised manager makes the offer

blocks.p: An **induction** introduces a new worker to the workplace, its safety rules and their job. It keeps them safe in the first days, when new people are most likely to be hurt, and gets them working well sooner.

head: An induction covers
Examples
rows: Tour; who's who; who to go to with problems
Exits, extinguishers, first aid, the assembly point, how to raise the alarm
Hot-work rules, permits, the machines they may use, PPE to wear and how to get it
Duties, targets, the quality standard, how work is recorded
Hours, breaks, overtime, leave, reporting sick, conduct

ul: Pair the new person with an experienced worker (a buddy) for the first days or weeks.
Check what they have understood, and check their first jobs.
Keep a signed record of the induction.

blocks.p: A **skills matrix** lists each team member against the skills the work needs (for example MMAW plate, MIG, aluminium TIG, 6G pipe, plasma cutting, reading drawings), showing who can do each task, who is learning, and who needs training. Compare it with what the plan needs, for example a new aluminium contract, and arrange coaching on the job, in-house training, courses through HEART/NSTA Trust and other providers, or qualification tests. Keep training records and review each person's progress.

blocks.h: When someone is not meeting targets

ul: Talk privately first, and stick to the facts.
Listen: the cause may be the equipment, materials, an unclear target, missing training, or a health or personal problem.
Agree what will change, what support you will give, and when you will review it.
Follow up, record what was agreed, and follow the workplace's policy if formal steps are needed.
Treat everyone the same way.

head: Record
How to keep it
rows: One agreed place; each issue has a version number and date, and a note of what changed; old copies removed
What changed, why, who agreed it, and when
Personal and confidential: locked away or password-protected, open only to authorised staff, kept accurate and up to date, as the data protection law requires
Signed, dated, kept with the staff file

head: Version
Date
Change
Agreed by
rows: Truss delivery moved to 28 Feb at the client's request

blocks.p: If the first issue is version 1 and the plan has been changed three times, the current one is version 4.

A chart with tasks down the side and time across, showing when each task happens

c1.title: Planning a quarter in Hayes
c1.text: Marlon is the Level 3 leading hand at a fabrication shop in Hayes, Clarendon. The owner's three-year business plan aims to win more school and church roofing work. For January to March the shop has orders for 36 roof trusses for a school canteen in Four Paths, due on 28 February, and 40 window grilles. Last quarter 80% of jobs were delivered on time, and 12 of the 150 items inspected needed rework. The steel comes from importers in Kingston. The owner has asked Marlon to help draft the quarter's operational plan.

c2.title: Hurricane shutters in Port Maria
c2.text: A shop in Port Maria, St Mary, has an order for 60 steel hurricane shutters, to be delivered in 4 weeks. Each shutter needs 3.5 hours of welding. The shop's other work needs 40 welding hours a week. There are two welders, each working 40 hours a week. The plasma cutter is available 40 hours a week and is already booked for 26 hours; the shutters will add 12 hours a week of cutting.

c3.title: A budget review in Black River
c3.text: At a fabrication shop in Black River, St Elizabeth, Odane compares last month's spending with the budget. Steel: budget J$450,000, actual J$495,000. Consumables: budget J$80,000, actual J$68,000. Overtime: budget J$60,000, actual J$102,000. Maintenance: budget J$25,000, actual J$25,000. The steel supplier raised its price per tonne by 10% at the start of the month. The shop did the amount of work that was planned.

c4.title: Storm-season risks in Annotto Bay
c4.text: Shawn, the supervisor at a shop in Annotto Bay, St Mary, is updating the risk register for August to October. He scores likelihood and consequence from 1 to 5. A storm closing the shop for several days: likelihood 3, consequence 4. The MIG set breaking down: 2 and 3. Late steel deliveries: 4 and 3. Theft of welding cables: 2 and 2. The shop uses about 4 reels of MIG wire a week, the supplier takes 2 weeks to deliver, and the shop keeps 2 reels as safety stock.

c5.title: People and skills in Brown's Town
c5.text: A fabrication shop in Brown's Town, St Ann, has won a contract for aluminium railings for a villa development, starting next quarter. A new welder, Andre, starts work on Monday. Delroy, a reliable welder for six years, has missed his weekly output target for the last three weeks. The supervisor is preparing the staffing part of the plan.

questions.q: Marlon's first draft objective says "Improve delivery". Which rewrite makes it SMART?
o: Deliver every job much faster than we did last quarter
Raise on-time delivery from 80% to 95% of jobs by 31 March
Make sure the school is happy with how fast it gets its trusses
Improve delivery as far as possible over the coming months
questions.why: It is specific (on-time delivery), measurable (80% to 95%), achievable, relevant to the business plan, and has a date. The others have no number or no date, so nobody could tell whether they were met.

questions.q: Before fixing the dates in the plan, whom should Marlon ask about how long steel takes to arrive?
o: The welders who will cut and fit the trusses
The canteen's principal, who set the due date
The purchasing clerk and the steel importers
The owner, who wrote the three-year business plan
questions.why: The people who order and supply the steel know the real lead times. Consulting the right stakeholder for each fact makes the timeline realistic.

questions.q: The plan aims to cut rework from 8% to 4% of items. Which KPI tracks this best?
o: The number of trusses made each week
The total hours the welders work each week
The number of complaints from the school
The first-time pass rate at inspection
questions.why: Last quarter 12 of 150 items (8%) needed rework. The first-time pass rate, from the inspection records, measures exactly what the objective is about; the others measure something else.

questions.q: The school moves the truss deadline to 14 March, and the plan's dates are changed. What should Marlon do with the plan?
o: Write the new dates on his own copy and tell the welders
Issue a new version, noting the change and who agreed it
Keep the old dates so that the team works a little faster
Tell the team by word of mouth and leave the plan as it was
questions.why: A new version number, the date, what changed and who agreed it, with old copies removed, means everyone works from the same, current plan and the reason for the change is on record.

questions.q: How many welding hours a week is the shop short?
o: 52.5 hours a week
50 hours a week
2.5 hours a week
12.5 hours a week
questions.why: Shutters: 60 × 3.5 = 210 hours ÷ 4 weeks = 52.5 hours a week. Add the other work: 52.5 + 40 = 92.5 hours needed. Two welders give 80 hours, so the shop is 12.5 hours a week short (50 hours over the 4 weeks).

questions.q: Which is the most sensible way to cover the shortfall for these four weeks?
o: About six hours' approved overtime a week for each welder
Ask both welders to work through their lunch breaks unpaid
Save time on each shutter by skipping the final inspection
Accept the order and warn the client it is likely to be late
questions.why: A short-term gap of 12.5 hours a week can be covered by approved, paid overtime (or a temporary welder). Unpaid work breaks employment law, and skipping inspection puts quality at risk.

questions.q: What will the plasma cutter's utilisation be once the shutter cutting is added?
questions.why: (26 + 12) ÷ 40 × 100 = 95%. A machine that busy is a bottleneck: one breakdown stops the job, so plan its maintenance and know the back-up before work starts.

questions.q: By what percentage was overtime over budget?
questions.why: Variance = 102,000 − 60,000 = J$42,000. As a percentage of the budget: 42,000 ÷ 60,000 × 100 = 70% over. Dividing by the actual figure instead (41%) is a common mistake.

questions.q: Consumables came in J$12,000 under budget. What should Odane check before calling it a saving?
o: That stock was not run down and needed orders not held back
That the welders were not paid too much overtime last month
Nothing: spending under budget is always good news for a shop
That the steel price rise has been passed on to all the clients
questions.why: The same amount of work was done, so spending less on consumables may mean the store is running low or invoices are still to come. Find the reason before treating it as a real saving.

questions.q: What is the total variance for the month?
o: J$75,000 over, about 12%
J$75,000 over, about 11%
J$45,000 over, about 10%
J$87,000 over, about 14%
questions.why: Budget 450 + 80 + 60 + 25 = J$615,000; actual 495 + 68 + 102 + 25 = J$690,000. The variance is J$75,000 over, and 75,000 ÷ 615,000 × 100 = about 12%. Dividing by the actual gives 11%; leaving out the consumables underspend gives J$87,000.

questions.q: What should Odane do about the steel overspend?
o: Cut the steel used on every job by 10% so the budget is met next month
Move part of the overspend to the maintenance heading, which was on budget
Ask the welders to explain why they used so much more steel this month
Report the price rise as the cause, and update budgets and quotes
questions.why: J$495,000 is exactly 10% above J$450,000, matching the price rise, so usage was as planned. The cause is reported, and future budgets and quotes are updated; moving costs between headings hides the truth.

questions.q: Which two risks should Shawn deal with first?
o: The storm and the MIG set breakdown
The storm and the late steel deliveries
The late steel and the cable theft
The MIG set breakdown and the cable theft
questions.why: Likelihood × consequence gives: storm 3 × 4 = 12, late steel 4 × 3 = 12, MIG set 2 × 3 = 6, cable theft 2 × 2 = 4. The two scoring 12 come first.

questions.q: Which of these is a contingency plan rather than a control?
o: If the MIG set fails, switch its jobs to the MMAW sets
Have the MIG set serviced every month by the supplier's technician
Keep spare liners, contact tips and drive rolls in the store
Train a second welder to change liners and drive rolls
questions.why: A control acts beforehand to make the risk less likely or less serious, like servicing, spares and training. A contingency plan says what to do once it has happened: here, moving the work to other sets.

questions.q: At what stock level should a new order for MIG wire be placed?
o: 8 reels
6 reels
10 reels
12 reels
questions.why: Reorder level = usage × lead time + safety stock = 4 × 2 + 2 = 10 reels. Ordering at 8 would leave no safety stock if the delivery is late, which is likely in the storm season.

questions.q: In a private talk, Delroy says the MIG set in his bay keeps tripping out. What should the supervisor do?
o: Tell Delroy to work faster between trips so he makes up the lost output
Give him a written warning, as he has missed the target three weeks running
Have the set repaired, note the cause, and adjust his target meanwhile
Move Delroy elsewhere and put the new welder in that bay instead
questions.why: The shortfall has a cause outside Delroy's control. Fixing the equipment, recording the cause and setting a fair target meanwhile is just and solves the real problem; a warning would punish him for a faulty machine.

questions.q: What is the best way to make sure Andre works safely and well in his first week?
o: Give him the safety rules to read and let him start on his own
Let him start welding at once, as he holds a Level 2 certificate
Wait until the aluminium contract starts before showing him round
Induct him, pair him with a skilled welder, and check his work
questions.why: An induction covers emergencies, safety rules, PPE, his job and policies, and a buddy and early checks catch problems while he learns the shop's ways. A certificate does not tell him where the exits or the rules are.

questions.q: How should the supervisor find out which welders will need training for the aluminium contract?
o: Assume every welder can weld aluminium as well as they weld steel
Ask the villa developer which of the welders it would prefer
Check the team's skills matrix against the contract's needs
Wait to see who has trouble once the aluminium work begins
questions.why: A skills matrix shows who can already do each task and who needs training. Comparing it with the contract shows the gap early, so training can be arranged before the work starts.

questions.q: Which is the best way to show a month's tasks so the team can see who does what each week?
o: A pie chart of the hours each task needs
A bar chart with tasks, owners and weeks
A table of last month's KPI results
A list of every task in alphabetical order
questions.why: A bar (Gantt) chart shows each task, its owner and the weeks it runs, so overlaps, dependencies and deadlines are clear at a glance.

questions.q: Income from repair jobs was J$50,000 above budget last month. How is this variance described?
o: Adverse, because the actual figure is over the budget
Adverse, because the budget must have been set too low
Favourable, because income is higher than planned
Neither, as variances are only worked out for costs
questions.why: For income, more than budget is favourable; for costs, more than budget is adverse. Always ask whether the line is income or a cost before naming the variance.

questions.q: A rush order tempts the team to skip the hot-work permit and fire watch on a site job. What should the team leader do?
o: Keep both, and re-plan the work or report the delay
Skip them this once, as the client agreed to the rush
Skip the permit but keep an extinguisher close by
Let the most senior welder decide if they are needed
questions.why: Safety controls and the law are never dropped to meet a target. If the time cannot be found safely, the plan is changed or the delay reported to management.
